SMSD: Sequential Methods for Study Design

Source: R/SMSD-package.R
SMSD-package.Rd

Sequential procedures for planning a study whose sample size cannot be fixed in advance, because the population values that a sample size formula needs (a standard deviation, a correlation, the effect size itself) are unknown. Data are collected in stages, and after each stage a stopping rule computed from the data in hand says whether sampling can stop. The package covers accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE; Maxwell, Kelley, & Rausch, 2008), in which the goal is a confidence interval as narrow as requested; minimum risk point estimation (MRPE), in which the goal is the smallest combined cost of estimation error and of sampling; a procedure that spends a fixed budget across several groups; and the classical fixed width, bounded risk, and two stage procedures for a mean, a median, or a location parameter.

Getting Started

Three vignettes introduce the package.

  • vignette("introduction", package = "SMSD"): the overview.

  • vignette("step-by-step-sequential-workflow", package = "SMSD"): one study, from its pilot sample to its stopping point.

  • vignette("complete-tour", package = "SMSD"): the procedures one by one.

A reader who wants one function to begin with should begin with seq_aipe_smd, the standardized mean difference between two groups; its help page has a complete example.

How the Functions Fit Together

Every procedure has a function that returns its pilot (first stage) sample size, named *_pilot(), and a check function that takes the data collected so far and evaluates the stopping rule once. The user collects the pilot sample, calls the check function, and, while attr(out, "is_satisfied") is FALSE, collects more observations and calls it again. A check function does not prompt, print, or keep anything between calls: the user owns the sampling loop, and each call is a calculation on the data it is given.

A check function returns an object of class smsd_check: a data frame with the columns term and value, holding the estimate, its confidence limits where the procedure has an interval, and the sample size in hand beside the one the rule calls for, with the stopping decision and the targets as attributes. See smsd_check_methods.

A Narrow Confidence Interval for an Effect Size

Sequential AIPE: sampling stops at the first sample size that meets the stopping rule, and the confidence interval at that point is no wider than the requested full width. Each effect size has a pilot function, a check function, and a function that simulates the whole procedure.

Pilot sample sizeCheckSimulation
seq_aipe_smd_pilotseq_aipe_smdseq_aipe_smd_sensitivity
seq_aipe_cv_pilotseq_aipe_cvseq_aipe_cv_sensitivity
seq_aipe_reg_coef_pilotseq_aipe_reg_coefseq_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity
seq_aipe_sm_pilotseq_aipe_smseq_aipe_sm_sensitivity
seq_aipe_c_pilotseq_aipe_cseq_aipe_c_sensitivity
seq_aipe_r_pilotseq_aipe_rseq_aipe_r_sensitivity
seq_aipe_R2_pilotseq_aipe_R2seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity
seq_aipe_gini_pilotseq_aipe_giniseq_aipe_gini_sensitivity

The effect sizes are the standardized mean difference (smd), the coefficient of variation (cv), the simple linear regression slope (reg_coef), the standardized mean (sm), and a contrast of group means (c), from Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018); the Pearson, Kendall, and Spearman correlations (r) and the squared multiple correlation (R2), from Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019); and the Gini index (gini), from Chattopadhyay and De (2016). The squared multiple correlation procedure assumes multivariate normality; the others assume no particular distribution. The point estimates gini_index, gini_mean_diff, and slr_slope are exported for use on their own.

Minimum Risk Point Estimation

Sampling stops when the estimated risk, the cost of estimation error plus the cost of the observations, is as small as it can be made.

Pilot sample sizeCheckSimulation
seq_mr_cv_pilotseq_mr_cvseq_mr_cv_sensitivity
seq_mr_smd_pilotseq_mr_smdseq_mr_smd_sensitivity

The coefficient of variation follows Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016). The standardized mean difference follows Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017), with one sampling cost or a different cost in each group; that article assumes normal populations with a common variance.

A Budget Across Groups

A contrast of several group means is estimated as precisely as a fixed budget allows when the groups differ in what an observation costs and in their unknown variances (Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, & Padalunkal, 2025).

seq_budget_optimalThe allocation if the standard deviations were known
seq_budget_pilotThe pilot sample size
seq_budgetThe check on the data collected so far
seq_budget_nextThe group that should receive the next observation
seq_budget_sensitivityA simulation of the whole procedure
decide_seq_budget_noninferiorityThe noninferiority test
decide_seq_budget_superiorityThe superiority test
decide_seq_budget_inferiorityThe inferiority test
decide_seq_budget_equivalenceThe equivalence test

The four tests are one-sided and are applied once sampling has ended.

Classical Procedures for a Mean, a Median, or a Location

These procedures are from Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009): confidence intervals of fixed width or bounded length, and point estimates with bounded or minimum risk. The purely sequential ones:

seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal gives the sample size that a known variance would give for the fixed width interval for a normal mean, and power_z gives the Type II error rate and the sample size of a one sample, one-sided z test. The negative exponential procedures estimate the location of that distribution.

Studying a Design Before Collecting Data

The *_sensitivity() functions linked above run a whole procedure, from its pilot sample to its stopping point, many times on simulated data with a known population value. They report the final sample size to expect and how much it varies, and, for the interval procedures, the width of the final interval and how often it contains the population value. The batch argument of the seq_aipe_* and seq_mr_* sensitivity functions shows what it costs to check the rule only after every several observations. Each help page lists the rows of its summary, which prints through smsd_sensitivity_methods.

Reading and Reporting a Result

Every check object has methods for print(), summary(), format(), and as.data.frame(), and for the tidy() and glance() generics of the generics package; see smsd_check_methods. SMSD does not export those two generics, so write generics::tidy(out) and generics::glance(out), or attach generics or broom first. seq_path applies a check function to data already in hand at each successive sample size and returns the whole stopping path; plot.smsd_path draws it, and smsd_path_methods documents its other methods. seq_report writes the paragraph, with its reference, that reports a check or a path in a methods or results section.

What the Procedures Guarantee

The seq_aipe_* procedures deliver the requested width by construction: whenever the stopping rule is met, the interval is no wider than width. Coverage is a different matter. It is an asymptotic property, which approaches the confidence level as the target narrows and the final sample grows, and it can fall well short of the confidence level when the target is wide, when the relationship studied is strong, or when a squared multiple correlation has many predictors. In 2,000 simulated studies each at the 95% level, with normal data unless noted, the final interval contained the population value in 0.94 of the studies for a standardized mean difference of 0.5 at a width of 0.8, in 0.78 for a Pearson correlation of 0.4 and in 0.70 for one of 0.8 at a width of 0.4, in 0.84 for a regression slope of 0.5 at a width of 0.4, in 0.79 for a coefficient of variation of 0.5 at a width of 0.2 with lognormal data, and in 0.36 for a squared multiple correlation of 0.5 with 15 predictors at a width of 0.3 (0.85 with 5 predictors). These figures have Monte Carlo standard errors between 0.005 and 0.011, so the figure that another help page reports for the same design, from another run, can differ in the second decimal. The help page of each check function states what its guarantee is, exact or asymptotic; the sensitivity functions measure it for the design at hand.

An Unusable Variance Estimate

In a small sample the estimate of the variance that a stopping rule needs can be zero, negative, or not finite. A check function then reports the stopping rule as not met and attaches a note, and its attribute variance_unusable is TRUE, so sampling continues; see smsd_check_methods. This is a deliberate departure from the stopping rules as printed in the source articles, under which a lower bound would stand in for such an estimate and the rule would be met at once with an interval far narrower than requested. A positive estimate, however small, is used as the articles prescribe. (In ts_fwd_norm_mean, ts_fwd_dfr_mean, ts_fwd_nexp_mean, and ts_br_norm_mean, a first stage with no variation is an error, because there the first stage variance or scale alone fixes the total sample size. ts_br_exp_mean uses the first stage mean and is not affected.)

Relation to DMAR

SMSD depends on the package DMAR, which is attached with it and provides the fixed sample size counterparts of the confidence interval procedures: ss_aipe_smd, ss_aipe_r, ss_aipe_R2, ss_aipe_cv, ss_aipe_reg_coef, ss_aipe_sm, and ss_aipe_c (there is none for the Gini index). If the population values are known well enough to fix the sample size in advance, use DMAR; if they are not, use SMSD.
